analysis.one_liner: Bans sitting members of Congress and senior congressional staff from trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The Ban Conflicted Trading Act drew 64 cosponsors from both parties but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit sitting members of Congress and senior congressional staff from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, or short positions, and from serving on the boards of for-profit companies. Members could keep pre-existing holdings only in a blind trust or sell them off, and violations would carry a civil penalty of at least 10 percent of the value of the illegal trade. The goal is to stop lawmakers from profiting on knowledge gained from their work, such as pending legislation or classified briefings. It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and received no further action of any kind.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors and the general public. Members of Congress often learn market-moving information through their work — upcoming legislation, regulatory decisions, closed-door briefings — and the bill would take that advantage off the table. It also lets everyday investors trade on the same footing as the people who write the rules for the markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday investors and the general public

how_it_helps.text: Bars sitting members of Congress and congressional officers and employees required to file financial disclosure reports from purchasing or selling securities, commodities, futures, or comparable derivative interests, or taking a net short position in any security.
Prohibits those same officials from serving as an officer or board member of any for-profit entity, closing a separate channel between their public role and private companies.

Allows existing holdings to be kept only in an ethics-committee-approved qualified blind trust, or sold within six months, so lawmakers retain widely held index funds and Treasury securities but cannot pick individual winners.
Enforces the ban with a civil penalty of at least 10 percent of the value of any prohibited trade, administered by the Senate and House ethics committees.

analysis.who_pays: Sitting members of Congress and senior congressional staff, who would have to divest individual holdings, place them in blind trusts, and give up personal trading and for-profit board seats. A small group of financial advisors who manage those personal accounts also lose the business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and senior staff

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is left to the House and Senate ethics committees — bodies made up of members of Congress themselves — which makes the ban dependent on self-policing by the people it restricts.

The penalty floor of 10 percent of the trade's value may be modest relative to what a well-timed trade on inside knowledge can earn, and the ethics committees can grant case-by-case exceptions such as approving blind trust arrangements.

A good-faith objection is that the ban reaches some officials well down the disclosure list and restricts personal financial choices, and blind trusts carry administrative costs for members who must set them up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but lopsided: members give up the ability to trade on information their positions give them, and the public gains a cleaner rule-making process and more trust in Congress. The honest weaknesses are in enforcement — the people being policed do the policing, the penalty floor is low, and exceptions are granted by the same ethics committees. Those are design problems worth fixing, not reasons to doubt that the restriction itself targets a genuine conflict.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the two-year Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the bill on March 3, 2021, joined by 14 original cosponsors including Democrats such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Joe Neguse and Republicans such as Matt Gaetz and Michael Cloud.

On introduction it was referred to the Financial Services Committee and, in addition, to the Agriculture and House Administration committees, a multi-committee referral that splits a bill among jurisdictions with no schedule for any of them.
On April 29, 2021 it was referred to the Financial Services subcommittee on Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit, and the record shows no further action after that.
The bill ended with 64 cosponsors, 61 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote in the House or Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress and senior congressional staff are better off: they kept the ability to trade individual stocks and serve on for-profit boards, and no new rules took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress and senior staff

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: 61 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining all or nearly all of its original Democratic sponsors.

for.name: 3 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Matt Gaetz and Michael Cloud.

for.name: Public advocacy groups and media coverage
for.what_they_did: Raised public pressure for a congressional stock-trading ban during 2021 and 2022 after reports of members trading stocks in sectors their committees oversee; several other trading-ban bills were introduced in the same period.

against.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Her committee took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was held in two years.

against.name: Rep. David Scott
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after its secondary referral.

against.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
against.what_they_did: Her committee, which shares jurisdiction over congressional ethics, took no action on the bill after referral.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill or any comprehensive congressional stock-trading ban to the House floor during the 117th Congress, despite dozens of cosponsors and sustained press attention; leadership favored no floor action on members' stock trading.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines — 61 Democrats and 3 Republicans, with Republicans Matt Gaetz and Michael Cloud among the original sponsors — but the bill died in committees controlled by the Democratic majority without any recorded vote, so party positions on the merits were never tested.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior congressional staff
industries.note: The bill would strip sitting lawmakers and senior staff of personal stock, commodity, and futures trading and for-profit board seats, ending their access to market moves informed by their work. Their institutional interest in keeping that trading runs against the public's interest in lawmakers not profiting from their offices.

A small segment of the wealth-management industry handles individual members' brokerage accounts and would lose that business if members had to divest or move to blind trusts. The impact is minor and the industry has no policy stake beyond losing these clients.
